data.title: Reconstructing the defences of Slavic hillforts
data.excerpt: The Slavs built no fortifications of mortared stone: their ramparts were boxes of oak beams filled with earth and stones, often with a dry-laid stone facing and a palisade on the crest. Together with Dwarf digital archeology we have visualised one possible variant of such a box rampart, and explain how it weathered into the simple mounds that can be seen on hillforts today.

blocks.text: The Slavs build most of their strongholds in this manner: they seek out meadows rich in water and thickets and mark out on them a round or square place, according to the shape and size they wish the stronghold to have. Then they dig all around and heap up the earth, which they strengthen with boards and stakes. In this way they form ramparts, which they build up until they have the required height. Then they measure out a gate for the stronghold on the convenient side and build a bridge up to it. By this they enter it.

children.text: The Slavs, and before them the Celts, the people of the Lusatian culture and other, older peoples, did not use stones bound with mortar to build their fortifications. For their defence they therefore built fortifications whose construction consisted of wooden beams tied to one another in various ways, between which the builders heaped earth and stones. Sometimes the front part, turned towards the enemy, was protected by a low stone wall (a stone facing), which was built of dry-laid stones and rested against the timber construction of the rampart. On the top of a rampart built in this way there was usually also a wooden palisade. The defenders standing on the rampart thus had the advantage of height over the enemy, and their bodies were directly protected by the wooden palisade. This type of rampart was also taken over by the early Hungarian state and was used until the Mongol invasion, when this type of fortification proved inadequate, since the Mongols were able to destroy timber-and-earth ramparts effectively. After their invasion King Béla IV therefore began to give massive support to the building of stone castles, which meant the decline of the building of timber-and-earth fortifications.

Hillforts played an important role in the history of Great Moravia. The Annals of Fulda, for example, write of the fortress of Devín, in which Rastislav fought against the Frankish king Louis. They also describe Rastislav's ineffable fortress (probably the hillfort of Mikulčice) and other fortified places, which caused the Franks and other attackers more than one furrowed brow. The building of hillforts is also archaeologically attested, above all in the course of the 9th century, when our ancestors often fought against the Frankish Empire, but also among themselves. At the beginning of the 10th century, after the death of King Svatopluk, the tribes of the Old Hungarians began to attack the territory of Great Moravia; some of its key centres they gradually conquered, others they obtained by agreement with local magnates who joined them, and Great Moravia broke up as a centralised state. At the beginning of the 10th century we therefore also find archaeological evidence of massive fires that destroyed some important hillforts, such as Mikulčice in Moravia or Bojná in Slovakia.

The construction of hillforts had various detailed technical solutions. We have tried to present to you one of the possible solutions of the method of building and construction of the defences – the box rampart. Strong oak beams, set vertically and anchored deep in the ground, were joined by horizontal beams, which created a wooden shuttering. Into the space thus created (the box) our ancestors gradually heaped earth and stones. The timber construction then held the earth in the required shape. On the top of the rampart thus created they placed a palisade, in such a way that it protected the whole body of the defender standing on the rampart, while at the same time it had gaps so that, if need be, the defender could shoot effectively with a bow from behind the palisade, throw javelins or strike directly at an enemy who had managed to climb right up onto the rampart.

The weakness of timber-and-earth hillforts was always their wooden construction. The Slavs and the older peoples therefore made use of the option of a low stone wall rested against the timber rampart, which considerably limited the chance for attackers to set the rampart on fire.

Nevertheless, some of the hillforts eventually succumbed to attack and were destroyed by fire. After such a destruction of a hillfort, when the wooden parts of the rampart had burnt, nothing held the rampart in its original shape any longer. After the demise of the hillfort the earthen part of the rampart and the stone facing therefore gradually weathered and lost their original shape and form. In the end, therefore, all that remained of the timber-and-earth rampart, whose contours had originally been defined by the timber and stone construction, was a simple mound, wider at the bottom and narrowing upwards. It is ramparts of this kind that we find today on the remains of ancient hillforts.

Dwarf digital archeology and Hradiska.sk have together attempted a reconstruction of one of the several possible variants of the construction of a hillfort. The video also briefly explains how, after many centuries, the ramparts visible today came out of such a rampart.
